topic: State health, biometric, AI and online laws

notes.front: What is the My Health My Data Act (MHMDA)?
notes.back: Washington's 2023 law, chapter 19.373 of the Revised Code of Washington, restricting how regulated entities collect, share and sell consumer health data.
notes.explanation: Its short title section says chapter 191, Laws of 2023, may be cited as the Washington my health my data act.
notes.example: Like HIPAA for health data held by apps and shops, but written by one state and aimed at businesses HIPAA does not reach.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.900
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is consumer health data under the My Health My Data Act?
notes.back: Personal information linked or reasonably linkable to a consumer that identifies their past, present or future physical or mental health status.
notes.explanation: The definition then lists examples of health status, from diagnoses to data inferred from non-health information.
notes.example: Like a medical record, but also the step count, period tracker or pharmacy purchase a shopping app holds.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.010(8)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a geofence under the My Health My Data Act?
notes.back: Technology using location signals, such as satellite positioning, cellular data or radio frequency identification, to set a virtual boundary round a place.
notes.explanation: For the Act, the virtual boundary must be 2,000 feet or less from the perimeter of the physical location.
notes.example: Like an invisible fence round a clinic that makes phones inside it light up with targeted adverts.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.010(14)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a bias audit under New York City's Local Law 144?
notes.back: An audit of an automated employment decision tool for bias, which must be done within one year before the tool is used.
notes.explanation: Employers and employment agencies may not use such a tool unless it has had a bias audit and information about it is public.
notes.example: Like an annual safety test for a lift, but checking a hiring tool for unfair results.
notes.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, Automated Employment Decision Tools (AEDT)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is automated decisionmaking technology (ADMT) under the CCPA regulations?
notes.back: Technology that processes personal information and uses computation to replace, or substantially replace, human decisionmaking.
notes.explanation: Substantially replacing means using the technology's output to decide without human involvement.
notes.example: Like a loan system that approves or declines applicants itself, with no one checking its output.
notes.source: CCPA Regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7000 et seq.), effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 7001 (definitions), p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: “Automated decisionmaking technology” or “ADMT” means any technology that processes personal information and uses computation to replace human decisionmaking or substantially replace human decisionmaking. (1) For purposes of this definition, to “substantially replace human decisionmaking” means a business uses the technology’s output to make a decision without human involvement.

notes.front: What are two examples of health status that make data consumer health data under the MHMDA?
notes.back: Any two of: health conditions or diagnoses; use or purchase of prescribed medication; reproductive or sexual health information; biometric or genetic data, among others.
notes.explanation: The statutory list is open: it says physical or mental health status includes, but is not limited to, its items.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.010(8)(b)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can data that is not itself about health be consumer health data under the MHMDA?
notes.back: Yes, when it is processed to associate a consumer with health data, including inferences drawn by algorithms or machine learning.
notes.explanation: The definition names proxy, derivative, inferred or emergent data derived from non-health information.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.010(8)(b)(xiii)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who is a 'consumer' under the My Health My Data Act?
notes.back: A Washington resident, or a natural person whose consumer health data is collected in Washington, acting in an individual or household context.
notes.explanation: People acting in an employment context are excluded.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.010(7)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A shopping app infers from a user's purchases of pregnancy tests and vitamins that she is pregnant. Under the MHMDA, what is the inference?
notes.back: C: Consumer health data, because it is derived from non-health data to associate her with a health status.
notes.choices:
A) Ordinary purchase history, outside the Act
B) Protected health information under HIPAA
C) Consumer health data
D) Publicly available information
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Act reaches inferences about health status. B: a shopping app is not a HIPAA covered entity. D: a private inference is not public.
notes.explanation: The definition covers inferred data, including data produced by algorithms or machine learning.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.010(8)(b)(xiii)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An Oregon resident visits Seattle and her period-tracking app collects her data while she is there. Is she a 'consumer' under the MHMDA?
notes.back: A: Yes, because her consumer health data is collected in Washington.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, her data is collected in Washington
B) No, only Washington residents are covered
C) No, because the app is based in Oregon
D) Only if she stays more than 30 days
notes.choicesExplained: B: residence is only one route into the definition. C: the app's base does not decide it. D: there is no length-of-stay test.
notes.explanation: The definition covers Washington residents and anyone whose consumer health data is collected in Washington.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.010(7)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When may a regulated entity collect consumer health data under the MHMDA?
notes.back: With the consumer's consent for a specified purpose, or to the extent necessary to provide a product or service the consumer requested.
notes.explanation: The same two routes apply to sharing, but sharing needs its own consent.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.030(1)(a)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What consent does the MHMDA require to share consumer health data?
notes.back: Consent that is separate and distinct from the consent to collect it, unless sharing is needed to provide a requested product or service.
notes.explanation: Consent must be obtained before the collection or sharing happens.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.030(1)(b)-(c)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A wellness app obtained consent to collect users' sleep data to show them sleep scores. It now wants to pass the data to an insurer partner. What does the MHMDA require?
notes.back: B: Separate consent to share, distinct from the collection consent.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing more, as consent was already given
B) Separate and distinct consent to share
C) Only a privacy policy update
D) Permission from the state health department
notes.choicesExplained: A: the collection consent does not cover sharing. C: notice alone is not consent. D: no such permission exists.
notes.explanation: Collection consent does not cover sharing; the Act requires a separate and distinct consent.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.030(1)(b)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What must a person obtain before selling consumer health data under the MHMDA?
notes.back: A valid authorisation signed by the consumer, separate from the consent to collect or share.
notes.explanation: The sale must stay within what the signed authorisation allows.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.070(1)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under the MHMDA, a valid authorisation to sell consumer health data must expire {{c1::one year}} from when the consumer signs it.
notes.back: one year
notes.explanation: The authorisation must state that expiry date.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.070(2)(h)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What must an MHMDA authorisation to sell consumer health data contain, among other things?
notes.back: The specific data to be sold, the names and contacts of seller and purchaser, and the purpose of the sale.
notes.explanation: It must also say that goods or services may not be conditioned on signing it, and that it can be revoked.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.070(2)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A fertility app wants to sell users' cycle data to a research broker. It adds a checkbox, pre-ticked, inside its terms of service. Is that enough under the MHMDA?
notes.back: D: No: it needs a separate valid authorisation signed by the consumer, with the contents the Act requires.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, a checkbox is consent
B) Yes, if the terms mention research
C) No, health data may never be sold
D) No, it needs a separate signed valid authorisation
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: a buried checkbox is not the separate signed authorisation. C: sale is allowed with a valid authorisation.
notes.explanation: A sale needs a signed valid authorisation that is separate from other consents.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.070(1)-(2)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For the MHMDA's geofence ban, a geofence is a virtual boundary {{c1::2,000 feet}} or less from the perimeter of the physical location.
notes.back: 2,000 feet
notes.explanation: The ban applies around entities that provide in-person health care services.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.010(14)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For which purposes is a geofence around an in-person health care provider unlawful under the MHMDA?
notes.back: To identify or track consumers seeking health care services, collect consumer health data, or send them health-related notifications or advertisements.
notes.explanation: The ban applies to 'any person', not only regulated entities.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.080
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An ad company draws a virtual boundary 1,500 feet round a Washington clinic and pushes adverts for pregnancy tests to phones inside it. What does the MHMDA say?
notes.back: C: It is unlawful: a geofence within 2,000 feet of an in-person health care provider used to send health-related adverts.
notes.choices:
A) Lawful, as adverts are not data collection
B) Lawful, if the boundary is over 1,000 feet
C) Unlawful geofencing
D) Lawful, if users can opt out later
notes.choicesExplained: A: sending health-related adverts is itself a banned purpose. B: the limit is 2,000 feet. D: the ban is not lifted by an opt-out.
notes.explanation: The boundary is within 2,000 feet and the purpose is a banned one.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.080
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the MHMDA characterise a violation for the purposes of Washington's Consumer Protection Act?
notes.back: As an unfair or deceptive act in trade or commerce and an unfair method of competition, not reasonable in relation to business development.
notes.explanation: The legislature also found the practices to be matters vitally affecting the public interest.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.090
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: unfair or deceptive acts or practices

notes.front: Sued under Washington's Consumer Protection Act for breaking the MHMDA, a company argues its practice was reasonable in relation to developing its business. Does that argument help it?
notes.back: A: No: the MHMDA declares that a violation is not reasonable in relation to the development and preservation of business.
notes.choices:
A) No, the Act declares violations not reasonable in relation to business development
B) Yes, it is a complete defence
C) Yes, if the company is a small business
D) Only if the attorney general agrees
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the Act rules the argument out for every regulated entity and small business. D: no such approval exists.
notes.explanation: The Act settles that point in advance for Consumer Protection Act purposes.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.373 (Washington My Health My Data Act), RCW 19.373.090
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do Washington's and Nevada's consumer health data laws differ on private lawsuits?
notes.back: Washington's is enforced through its Consumer Protection Act; Nevada's makes violations a deceptive trade practice and expressly creates no private right of action.
notes.explanation: Nevada's provisions say they do not create a private right of action.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.550
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Nevada's 2023 consumer health data law cover?
notes.back: Personally identifiable information that a regulated entity uses to identify a consumer's past, present or future health status.
notes.explanation: The provisions are sections 603A.400 to 603A.550 of the Nevada Revised Statutes, added to the Nevada Revised Statutes in 2023.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.430
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When may a regulated entity collect consumer health data under Nevada law?
notes.back: With the consumer's affirmative, voluntary consent, or to the extent necessary to provide a product or service the consumer requested.
notes.explanation: Sharing needs a separate consent, unless another route such as a legal requirement applies.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.500
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Nevada require before a person sells consumer health data?
notes.back: The consumer's written authorisation, and the sale must stay within it; goods or services may not be conditioned on it.
notes.explanation: The authorisation must be in plain language and contain listed items.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.535
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Nevada bans implementing a geofence within {{c1::1,750 feet}} of a medical facility or other in-person health care provider for tracking, collecting health data or targeted messages.
notes.back: 1,750 feet
notes.explanation: Washington's comparable limit is 2,000 feet.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.540
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Nevada company sells consumer health data without any authorisation. A customer wants to sue it under Nevada's consumer health data provisions. What does the law say?
notes.back: A: The violation is a deceptive trade practice, but those provisions create no private right of action.
notes.choices:
A) It is a deceptive trade practice, with no private right of action
B) She may sue for statutory damages
C) Only the FTC may act
D) The law has no enforcement mechanism
notes.choicesExplained: B: the provisions create no private right of action. C: the state deceptive trade practice law applies. D: violations are enforceable as deceptive trade practices.
notes.explanation: Nevada treats violations as deceptive trade practices and rules out private actions under these provisions.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.550
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do Washington's and Nevada's geofence bans around health care providers differ in distance?
notes.back: Washington's covers 2,000 feet or less from the location's perimeter; Nevada's covers 1,750 feet.
notes.explanation: Both ban geofences used to track consumers, collect health data or send health-related messages.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.540
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What must a website operator's notice under Nevada law disclose about tracking?
notes.back: Whether third parties may collect covered information about a consumer's online activities over time and across different websites.
notes.explanation: The notice must also list the categories of covered information collected and the third parties it may be shared with.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.340
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How can a consumer stop a website operator selling their covered information under Nevada law?
notes.back: By sending a verified request to the operator's designated request address; the operator must respond within 60 days.
notes.explanation: Once the request arrives, the operator must not sell covered information it has collected or will collect about that consumer.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.345
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which advertising falls outside the Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act's 'targeted advertising'?
notes.back: Ads based on activity within the controller's own sites or apps, and contextual ads based on the current search or visit, among others.
notes.explanation: Targeted advertising means ads chosen from activity over time and across nonaffiliated websites or apps.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-575
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Virginia news site shows a reader a car advert because she is reading an article about cars, using nothing else about her. Is this targeted advertising under the VCDPA?
notes.back: B: No: ads based on the context of the current visit are excluded.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, every personalised ad is targeted
B) No, contextual ads are excluded
C) Yes, because it uses personal data
D) Only if she is logged in
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the definition excludes contextual ads. D: being logged in does not decide it.
notes.explanation: Targeted advertising requires data from activities over time across nonaffiliated sites or apps.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-575
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Nevada website operator receives a verified request not to sell a consumer's covered information. How long does it have to respond?
notes.back: D: 60 days after receiving it.
notes.choices:
A) 10 days
B) 30 days
C) 45 days
D) 60 days
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: Nevada's operator response period is 60 days; 45 days is the figure in California and Virginia.
notes.explanation: Nevada allows a response period of 60 days, with a possible extension.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.345(4)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Washington's biometric law exclude from 'biometric identifier'?
notes.back: Physical or digital photographs, video or audio recordings and data generated from them, and HIPAA health care information.
notes.explanation: A biometric identifier is data from automatic measurement of biological characteristics, such as fingerprints or irises, used to identify a person.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.375 (biometric identifiers), RCW 19.375.010(1)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What must a person do before enrolling a biometric identifier in a database for a commercial purpose under Washington law?
notes.back: Give notice, obtain consent, or provide a mechanism to prevent later use of the identifier for a commercial purpose.
notes.explanation: The exact notice and consent needed depend on the context.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.375 (biometric identifiers), RCW 19.375.020(1)-(2)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is notice and consent needed under Washington's biometric law to enrol a biometric identifier for a security purpose?
notes.back: No. The law does not require notice and consent for enrolment in furtherance of a security purpose, such as preventing shoplifting or fraud.
notes.explanation: Security purposes include protecting accounts, software and online services.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.375 (biometric identifiers), RCW 19.375.020(7) and 19.375.010(8)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who enforces Washington's biometric identifier law?
notes.back: Solely the attorney general, under the Consumer Protection Act.
notes.explanation: Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.375 (biometric identifiers), RCW 19.375.030
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: unfair or deceptive acts or practices

notes.front: A Washington gym enrols members' fingerprints for entry and now wants to sell the templates to a marketing firm. What does the law require first?
notes.back: C: The members' consent, since disclosure for a commercial purpose needs consent unless an exception applies.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, as the gym already holds them
B) Only a notice on the website
C) The members' consent
D) Approval from the state health department
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: sale for a commercial purpose needs consent. D: no such approval exists.
notes.explanation: Without consent, an enrolled identifier may not be sold or disclosed for a commercial purpose except in listed cases.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.375 (biometric identifiers), RCW 19.375.020(3)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Washington shop keeps ordinary security-camera video of customers but runs no identification on it. Is the video a 'biometric identifier' under Washington's biometric law?
notes.back: A: No: video recordings and data generated from them are excluded.
notes.choices:
A) No, video recordings are excluded
B) Yes, any image of a person is biometric
C) Yes, if kept for more than 30 days
D) Only if the shop sells the video
notes.choicesExplained: B: the law excludes photographs and video. C and D: neither retention time nor sale changes the definition.
notes.explanation: The definition excludes photographs and video or audio recordings.
notes.source: Revised Code of Washington, chapter 19.375 (biometric identifiers), RCW 19.375.010(1)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides the bias audit itself, what must be public before a New York City employer uses an AEDT?
notes.back: Information about the bias audit; the city's complaint page refers to posting a summary of the audit results.
notes.explanation: Required notices to employees or job candidates are a further condition.
notes.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, Automated Employment Decision Tools (AEDT)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A New York City employment agency's hiring tool had a bias audit two years ago. It wants to keep using the tool. What does Local Law 144 require?
notes.back: B: A new bias audit, since the audit must be within one year of the tool's use.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, one audit lasts for good
B) A bias audit within one year of use
C) A licence from the state
D) Only a notice to candidates
notes.choicesExplained: A: the audit must be within one year of use. C: no licence is required. D: notice is needed as well as, not instead of, a recent audit.
notes.explanation: An older audit no longer meets the one-year condition.
notes.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, Automated Employment Decision Tools (AEDT)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a 'significant decision' for the CCPA's ADMT rules?
notes.back: A decision that provides or denies financial or lending services, housing, education, employment or contracting opportunities or pay, or healthcare services.
notes.explanation: The list covers finance, housing, education, work and healthcare decisions.
notes.source: CCPA Regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7000 et seq.), effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 7001 (definitions), p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: “Significant decision” means a decision that results in the provision or denial of financial or lending services, housing, education enrollment or opportunities, employment or independent contracting opportunities or compensation, or healthcare services.

notes.front: By when must a business already using ADMT for significant decisions comply with the CCPA's ADMT article?
notes.back: No later than 1 January 2027.
notes.explanation: Businesses already using ADMT before that date had until then to comply.
notes.source: CCPA Regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7000 et seq.), effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 7200(b), p. 91
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: A business that uses ADMT for a significant decision prior to January 1, 2027, must be in compliance with the requirements of this Article no later than January 1, 2027.

notes.front: What notice must a business give before using ADMT for a significant decision?
notes.back: A Pre-use Notice about its use of ADMT and consumers' rights to opt out of and access ADMT.
notes.explanation: It may be given within the notice at collection if that notice includes the required information.
notes.source: CCPA Regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7000 et seq.), effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 7220(a), p. 92
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: must provide consumers with a Pre-use Notice. The Pre-use Notice must inform consumers about the business’s use of ADMT and consumers’ rights to opt-out of ADMT and to access ADMT, as set forth in this section. A business may provide a Pre-use Notice in its Notice at Collection

notes.front: When need a business not offer an opt-out of ADMT for a significant decision, among other exceptions?
notes.back: When it offers an appeal to a human reviewer who has authority to overturn the decision.
notes.explanation: The reviewer must have the authority to overturn the decision.
notes.source: CCPA Regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7000 et seq.), effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 7221(b)(1), p. 94
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: The business provides the consumer with a method to appeal the decision to a human reviewer who has the authority to overturn the decision.

notes.front: What must a business explain in response to a request to access ADMT?
notes.back: The specific purpose for using ADMT, the logic of the ADMT, and the outcome, in plain language.
notes.explanation: The purpose may not be described generically, such as 'to improve our services'.
notes.source: CCPA Regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7000 et seq.), effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 7222(b), p. 97
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: (1) The specific purpose for which the business used ADMT with respect to the consumer. The business must not describe the purpose in generic terms, such as “to improve our services.” (2) Information about the logic of the ADMT.

notes.front: Must a consumer verify their identity to opt out of ADMT under the CCPA regulations?
notes.back: No. Businesses may not require identity verification for ADMT opt-outs, just as for opt-outs of sale or sharing and requests to limit.
notes.explanation: The same section requires a reasonable verification method for requests to delete, correct, know or access ADMT.
notes.source: CCPA Regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7000 et seq.), effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 7060, p. 64
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: request to know, or request to access ADMT is the consumer about whom the business has collected information. (b) A business shall not require a consumer to verify their identity to make a request to opt- out of sale/sharing, to make a request to limit, or to make a request to opt-out of ADMT.

notes.front: A California employer uses ADMT to reject job applicants with no human involvement and offers no appeal. What must it offer applicants under the CCPA regulations?
notes.back: C: The ability to opt out of ADMT for that decision.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, hiring is exempt
B) Only a notice after the decision
C) The ability to opt out of ADMT
D) A right to sue for damages
notes.choicesExplained: A: employment opportunities are significant decisions. B: a Pre-use Notice comes before use, and the opt-out is still needed. D: the regulations set rights, not a damages claim.
notes.explanation: Without a qualifying human appeal or another exception, the opt-out right applies.
notes.source: CCPA Regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7000 et seq.), effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 7221(a), p. 94
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: A business must provide consumers with the ability to opt-out of the use of ADMT to make a significant decision concerning the consumer, except as set forth in subsection (b).

notes.front: A lender answers a consumer's request to access ADMT by saying it used the tool 'to improve our services'. Is that enough?
notes.back: D: No: the specific purpose must be given, not a generic description.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, any purpose statement will do
B) Yes, if the privacy policy says more
C) No, it must also pay compensation
D) No, it must state the specific purpose
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: generic purposes are ruled out, and the response must be individual. C: no compensation is required.
notes.explanation: The regulations give 'to improve our services' as an example of a forbidden generic purpose.

notes.front: What does Colorado's Senate Bill 21-169 forbid insurers to do?
notes.back: Unfairly discriminate on protected traits in any insurance practice, or use external consumer data, algorithms or predictive models that unfairly discriminate on them.
notes.explanation: Protected traits include race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion, sex, sexual orientation, disability, gender identity and gender expression.
notes.source: Colorado General Assembly, SB21-169 Restrict Insurers' Use of External Consumer Data, bill summary
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What must Colorado insurers maintain under the rules required by Colorado's Senate Bill 21-169?
notes.back: A risk management framework reasonably designed to find whether their use of external data sources unfairly discriminates.
notes.explanation: They must also report the results, explain their use of external data, and have the chief risk officer attest.
notes.source: Colorado General Assembly, SB21-169 Restrict Insurers' Use of External Consumer Data, bill summary
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Colorado car insurer adopts a pricing model built on purchased consumer data. Testing suggests it unfairly disadvantages drivers of one ethnic origin. What does Colorado's Senate Bill 21-169 require?
notes.back: A: The insurer must not use it in a way that unfairly discriminates, and must work under its risk management framework and the commissioner's rules.
notes.choices:
A) It must not use the model in a way that unfairly discriminates
B) It may use it if the data was bought lawfully
C) It may use it for car insurance only
D) It need only tell customers about the model
notes.choicesExplained: B: lawful purchase does not permit unfair discrimination. C: the ban covers any insurance practice. D: disclosure does not cure unfair discrimination.
notes.explanation: Using an external data source or model that unfairly discriminates on ethnic origin is prohibited.
notes.source: Colorado General Assembly, SB21-169 Restrict Insurers' Use of External Consumer Data, bill summary
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
